headline: Bunker Balls Tighten From Oyster Bay to Stratford Shoal — Bass Finally Committing
subhead: The new moon squeezed the bait hard this week, and for the first time this fall the stripers are eating with real intent instead of just picking at stragglers.
body_markdown:
The bunker told the story before the boats did. Since Tuesday, big pods of adult bunker have been pinching up tight against the beaches and river mouths from Oyster Bay through the Norwalk Islands, with smaller peanut schools stacking inside Port Jeff Harbor and along the flats off Charles Island. Terns have been working low and nervous over the same water for three straight mornings, which is usually the tell that something bigger is pushing from underneath. It was.

The September 10 new moon delivered the hardest tidal push of the young fall season, and that extra current did exactly what it's supposed to do — it squeezed bait against structure and gave stripers a reason to commit instead of just nosing around the edges. We flagged this pattern last week, saying bass were shifting into classic early-fall staging as bunker schools tightened under the building moon, and this week is the first real confirmation of it. Reports out of the Norwalk Islands and off Stratford Shoal describe bass finally driving bait to the surface in short, violent windows rather than the scattered pecking that's defined most of late August.

The thermal setup is helping concentrate where that action is happening. Kings Point on the western end is reading close to 71 degrees, while New London out east has slipped to the high 60s. That west-to-east gradient means the warmer, bait-loaded water from Oyster Bay through the Norwalk Islands is holding the most consistent feeding activity right now, while the Stratford Shoal and Middle Ground Light stretch is a step behind but should catch up as the moon eases off its peak and bait keeps sliding east with it.

Bass are running mostly schoolie to mid-20-inch class through the Norwalk Islands, with the better fish — some pushing high-20s to low-30s — showing on the last two hours of the ebb around the Stratford Shoal rip, where the current rips hard enough to hold bait against the rockpile. Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig in 15 to 25 feet have been the most consistent producer there, but when the surface activity breaks — and it has been breaking in short, unpredictable windows around dawn and again at dusk — a white bucktail with a curl-tail trailer worked through the melee will draw fast strikes. Around Charles Island and the flats off Milford, smaller bass and snapper blues are mixing into the same bait, and a 1-ounce bucktail bounced along the bottom on the last of the outgoing has been drawing steady, if not spectacular, action.

Bluefish are the more reliable story right now. Snapper blues are thick in the back bays from Oyster Bay through the Norwalk Islands — good news for anyone breaking in a kid on light spinning gear — and that snapper density has historically been the early tell for adult blues showing up in bigger numbers, which is starting to play out. A near-19-pound bluefish taking down a big derby prize out at Montauk this week confirms the pattern the whole region is riding: bait stacking tight to structure as surface water starts to ease off summer highs, and blues piling on top of it. Expect more adult blues to filter into the Central Sound over the next week or two as that cooling trend continues to build.

Fluke are the honest disappointment of the week. The keeper-grade bite has largely evacuated the Central Sound — most of what's coming over the rail around the Norwalk Islands and outside Port Jeff Harbor is short fish, with the better fluke already staging toward deeper, cooler water ahead of their fall exit. That lines up with what we called last week — expect the tapering to continue as water eases through September and the bigger fish keep heading offshore. If fluke is the target, focus effort on deeper drop-offs outside the harbor mouths rather than the shallow flats that produced all summer.

Porgies remain the most dependable meat in the boat right now. The reef structure off the Norwalk Islands and the rockpiles around Middle Ground Light are still loaded, and bloodworms or clam on a high-low rig in 20 to 35 feet will fill a cooler without much fuss. Blackfish are starting to show as the water eases into their preferred range — still early, but worth checking structure spots you'd normally save for October with a green crab on a jig head.

Looking ahead, the moon is moving off its new phase, which should ease tidal energy slightly over the next several days but not kill the pattern — the bunker migration underneath it is the real driver, and that's not going anywhere yet. The next best window looks like the last two hours of the ebb through the weekend, particularly around Stratford Shoal and the Norwalk Islands, where warmer water and concentrated bait are lining up. If the wind stays out of the south and holds the water clean, this could be the week the Central Sound blitz pattern finally stretches from a few lucky mornings into something anglers can plan around.
